html:
The five Muslim-ruled kingdoms of the Deccan plateau in south-central India that grew out of the break-up of the Bahmani Sultanate around 1500, and lasted until the Mughals swallowed them in the 1600s.

  • Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi dynasty), from 1490.
  • Bijapur (Adil Shahi dynasty), from 1490.
  • Berar (Imad Shahi dynasty), from 1490.
  • Golconda (Qutb Shahi dynasty), from 1518.
  • Bidar (Barid Shahi dynasty), from the 1520s.

They fought each other constantly, but in 1565 they joined forces and crushed Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota, then sacked its capital. The smaller states were soon absorbed by the bigger: Berar by Ahmadnagar, Bidar by Bijapur. The Mughal Empire took Ahmadnagar in stages up to 1636, and Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur in 1686 and Golconda in 1687.

Their courts mixed Persian, Turkish, African and local Indian cultures. They produced Dakhni, an early form of Urdu, a school of painting, and buildings such as the Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur and the Charminar of Hyderabad. Golconda's mines were famed for diamonds.
sum: The five Muslim-ruled kingdoms of the Deccan plateau in south-central India that grew out of the break-up of the Bahmani Sultanate around 1500, and lasted until the Mughals swallowed them in the 1600s.
